title: Bil-bēt — home and what's in it
goal: Describe where you live, say where things are, and handle renting from first questions to complaints.
bekal: name the rooms and furniture in a home
describe where things are with the right preposition
handle renting: ask, bargain, and report something broken

dialogs.title: حَكِي — شَقَّة لَلْإِيجَار
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking at a small apartment with its owner, Umm Rami.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: Come in, this is the apartment.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Nice. How many rooms are there?

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: Two bedrooms, a living room, a kitchen, and a bathroom.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.text: إِيه. فِي تَخِت وْخَزَانِة وْطَاوْلِة وْكَرَاسِي.
lines.baca: ēh. fi takht w khazaane w ṭaawle w karaasi.
lines.id: Yes. There's a bed, a wardrobe, a table, and chairs.
lines.literal: yes. there-is bed and wardrobe and table and chairs.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: And the kitchen? Is there a fridge?

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.text: فِي بَرَّاد وْغَاز. بَسّ مَا فِي غَسَّالِة.
lines.baca: fi barraad w ghaaz. bass ma fi ghassaale.
lines.id: There's a fridge and a stove. But no washing machine.
lines.literal: there-is fridge and gas. but not there-is washer.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: OK. How much is the rent a month?

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: Two hundred, and electricity is on you.

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.text: اَلْمَي عَلَيِّي. بَسّ لَازِم تِدْفَع شَهْرَين مُقَدَّم.
lines.baca: el-mayy ‘aleyyi. bass laazim tidfa‘ shahrēn mu’addam.
lines.id: Water's on me. But you have to pay two months in advance.
lines.literal: the-water on-me. but must you-pay two-months in-advance.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Two months is a lot. Could it be one?

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: All right, since you're a student. One month.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Thank you. When can I move in?

lines.speaker: أُمّ رَامِي:
lines.id: From the start of the month. Make yourself at home.

notes: **The phrase اَلْبَيْت بَيْتَك is as Levantine as it gets.** Literally "the house is your house," it's what hosts say to guests and landlords to tenants. The reply: يِسْلَمُوا or اَللَّه يْخَلِّيلَك يَاه.

**With money, عَلَيْك means "on you."** اَلْكَهْرَبَا عَلَيْك means the electricity is your responsibility. In reverse, عَلَيِّي means "it's on me," which is exactly what someone says when they want to pay for your meal at a restaurant.

**The word صَالُون means living room**, and it came from French by way of Lebanon. In Jordan you'll also hear غُرْفَة الْجُلُوس. Levantine homes almost always have a separate living room for guests, and it's central to the etiquette of hospitality.

**The word مَفْرُوش means "furnished," and it's a must-ask question when looking for a place.** The feminine form is مَفْرُوشَة, and the opposite is عَ الْعَظِم (literally "on the bone," meaning completely bare).

**Paying in advance is normal throughout the Levant.** One to three months is usual, and it's negotiable — especially if you're a student. The لَإِنِّي طَالِب argument really works and isn't seen as demeaning.

**The word شَقَّة means apartment, and بَيْت means house or home in general.** People in the Levant call their own apartment بَيْت without a second thought, just as English speakers say "home" for wherever they live.

grammars.title: Describing where things are, step by step
body: The prepositions from unit 11 now go to work around the house, and they can take possessive endings to point to yourself.

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: the bed is next to the window
the wardrobe is behind the door
the books are on the table
the bag is under the bed
the kitchen is in front of me
the bathroom is at the end of the hall
the fridge is inside the kitchen

after: To ask, just replace the location with وَين — for example وَين الْخَزَانِة؟ The answer is preposition + place, with no verb needed at all.

To say something "is in" a place, use فِي from unit 5 followed by the place: فِي بَرَّاد بِالْمَطْبَخ ("there's a fridge in the kitchen"). The difference from the table: this one introduces the thing, while the table places things already known.

grammars.title: Adjectives for where you live
after: Adjectives always come **after** the noun, the reverse of English: بَيْت كْبِير ("a big house"), أُوضَة نْضِيفَة ("a clean room").

⚠️ If the noun has اَل, the adjective **must** have اَل too — for example اَلْبَيْت الْكْبِير ("the big house"). Without اَل on the adjective, it turns into a sentence: اَلْبَيْت كْبِير ("the house is big"). This difference matters and is often missed.

blocks.text: The word ضَوّ means both "light" and "electricity" in everyday use. رَاح الضَّوّ ("the power's out") is one of the most common sentences in Syria and Lebanon, and you'll hear it several times a day.

blocks.title: Complaining and asking for repairs
items: The pattern: فِي مُشْكِلِة بِالـ… — for example فِي مُشْكِلِة بِالسَّخَّان ("there's a problem with the water heater").
If something's broken: اَلْبَرَّاد خَرْبَان *el-barraad kharbaan* ("the fridge is broken"). خَرْبَان is used for anything that doesn't work.
To ask for a repair: مُمْكِن تْصَلِّحُو؟ *mumkin tṣallho?* ("can you fix it?"). Add لَو سَمَحْت and you're always safe.

blocks.text: The word وَلَّا *walla* means "or" in either-or questions, and it's different from وَاللَّه *walla* meaning "by God" — two words that look alike and are told apart by context. For "or" in ordinary statements, Levantine Arabic uses أَو.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three things to ask that people often forget
items: **Electricity and water.** In Syria and Lebanon, scheduled power cuts are common, and many buildings have a separate generator subscription: فِي اِشْتِرَاك مُوَلِّدَة؟
**The water heater.** Ask whether it's electric or gas: اَلسَّخَّان كَهْرَبَا وَلَّا غَاز؟ It decides your monthly costs.
**A written contract.** Verbal rentals are common among students, but at least ask for a receipt: مُمْكِن وَصِل؟
How many rooms are there in this apartment?
How much is the rent a month?
The room is clean and spacious.
